cues.text: A boy and a ball
Ronaldo Luís Nazário de Lima was born in 1976.
He grew up in Bento Ribeiro, a suburb of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, and played football in the streets with friends.
When Ronaldo was eleven, his parents separated.
That can be a very hard change for any child.
Ronaldo kept playing, and at twelve he joined a futsal team called Social Ramos.
Open the futsal hall doors.
In his first season he scored 166 goals, a city youth record.
He later called futsal his first love.
When your family changes, it’s okay to feel sad or mixed up. Friends and the things you love can help.
The bus fare
Ronaldo supported Flamengo, a big club in Rio.
But the bus ride to their practice took an hour, and he could not afford the fare.
He missed practice, and Flamengo turned him down.
But Jairzinho, a former Brazil player who coached the small club São Cristóvão, had seen how good Ronaldo was.
Ronaldo played for its youth teams, and Jairzinho helped him move to the club Cruzeiro.
Turn the bus sign to a new road.
In 1994, at seventeen, Ronaldo was the youngest player in the Brazil squad that won the World Cup.
A no is not the end. When someone believes in you, let them help you find another way.
Hours before the final
At the 1998 World Cup, people called Ronaldo the best player in the world.
He scored four goals and helped Brazil reach the final against France.
But hours before the final, Ronaldo suddenly became very ill.
He was taken off the team sheet, but he said he felt fine and asked to play, so the coach put him back in.
He did not play like himself, and Brazil lost 3–0.
Lift the golden ball.
He was still named the best player of the tournament.
Ronaldo later said, “We lost the World Cup but I won another cup – my life.”
Your health matters more than any game. You are more than one result.
The knee that gave way
In 1999 Ronaldo was playing for Inter Milan in Italy.
In November, during a match against Lecce, his knee buckled, and he had to limp off.
A tendon in his knee was torn, and he needed an operation.
Five months later, on 12 April 2000, he came back.
After only six minutes, his knee gave way again, even worse than before.
The injury could have ended his career.
Lift the rain cloud.
Ronaldo had a long road ahead, but this was not the end of his story.
Sometimes a setback happens twice. It’s okay to feel sad, and it’s okay to rest and heal.
Step by step
Getting better took a long time.
Ronaldo had two operations, and then rehabilitation: months of exercises that help a body heal.
A French surgeon, Gérard Saillant, operated on his knee, and a medical team helped him recover.
He missed the whole 2000 to 2001 season.
While he was away, his teammate Javier Zanetti became the captain.
Climb the three steps.
In late 2001, Ronaldo became Inter’s captain.
He said he used to picture the World Cup trophy in front of his eyes, and imagine holding it up.
Healing takes time. Take one small step at a time, and let people help you.
The comeback
Ronaldo had missed all of Brazil’s qualifying games, but he was ready for the 2002 World Cup in South Korea and Japan.
He scored eight goals, more than any other player.
In the final against Germany, in Yokohama, he scored twice, and Brazil won 2–0.
Lift the World Cup trophy.
Ronaldo was the first player to go and comfort the German players.
His surgeon was in the crowd as his guest.
Ronaldo later dedicated his World Player of the Year award to the medical team who helped him recover.
A setback isn’t the end of the story. When you win, be kind, and thank the people who helped you.
